prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock and its development, with many atoms interrogated at once, to fractional uncertainties near 10^-18, which has opened laboratory tests of gravitational redshift and of fundamental physics

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: optical lattice clocks as the sole prize part, credited to Katori and Ye. What has changed is the reason I am confident. After the first round, six of us name the same pair and the same science, and I treat that as a prompt to test the case against its own caveats, not as evidence. The test I apply as an atomic theorist is simple. A physical idea has to remove a specific obstacle, and the result has to survive comparison between laboratories that did not share systematics. The obstacle was that a trapping laser shifts the very transition one wants to measure, and that shift would swamp any gain from holding many atoms. Katori's magic-wavelength condition cancels it to first order, so thousands of atoms can be probed at once, and that is what turned the optical clock from a single-particle instrument into a statistical one. Ye's group then showed what the regime could deliver: systematic uncertainty and stability near 10^-18, millimetre-scale gravitational redshift across an atomic sample, and the use of many-body interactions inside the clock. Strontium, ytterbium and other lattice clocks in several countries now agree at that level, which is the robustness I need. On the chair's question about a one-sentence distinction, my answer is this. The 2005 prize honoured the comb, a ruler for optical frequencies. The 2012 prize honoured control of single quantum systems, ions included. This prize would honour the first scheme in which a large ensemble of neutral atoms is held in light without disturbing the clock transition, which is a different mechanism and has opened measurements, redshift, constants and dark-matter couplings, that neither earlier prize made possible. I judge it a discovery about how to make atoms behave as ideal quantum oscillators in a perturbing field, and the observations that followed show it is more than a technique. I would write the citation on demonstrated performance and not on a redefinition of the second, which is a decision for metrologists. I do not think a second prize part should be added: with two names used, only one person remains, and no shortlisted candidate fits in that space without a credit I cannot defend.
statement.case_against: The objection I take most seriously is still lineage, because Ye shared the 2005 prize and the clock story already carries two Nobel prizes. If the committee decides that time metrology has been rewarded enough, I have no scientific reply, only the argument that the lattice regime is a distinct step. Second, Olsson's priority point is real. From memory, Katori's group proposed the state-insensitive lattice around 2001 to 2003 and demonstrated the first strontium lattice clock in 2005, while Lemonde and colleagues in Paris worked on lattice schemes in parallel in the same years, and the Ye group's own early work explored state-insensitive traps in parallel. I have not checked the original papers, and I will not claim a clean priority that I cannot show. Third, a clock can be read as an instrument and not as an observation of nature, which is Mehlig's and Pearce's point. Finally, the pair leaves out the wider strontium and ytterbium community, and the citation has to be precise about what it credits so that it does not appear to claim the whole field.

responses.point: Olsson wants the priority between Katori's proposal and first demonstration and Ye's later, more accurate realisation reviewed before the pair is accepted without qualification, and asks that Kroll and I report the early-2000s chronology.
responses.response: I can give the chronology only from memory, and I say so plainly: the committee should check the original papers before the vote. As I recall it, Katori's group published the engineered light-shift trap proposal and its first strontium lattice clock demonstration in the early to mid 2000s, and parallel proposals, notably from the Paris group around Lemonde, treated the same idea for alkaline-earth atoms but did not produce the first operating lattice clock. The Ye group then reached the accuracy records. That sequence supports your own criterion, because it does not make the second group a mere improvement on the first. Katori holds the concept and first clock, and Ye holds the decisive demonstration of what the regime can reach, including the redshift and many-body results. I would therefore keep both names, but I would write the citation as 'invention and development' so that it does not claim a single origin for every step. If the chronology check shows a parallel claimant with a genuinely equal contribution, I would reconsider the pair, not the topic.

responses.point: Mehlig keeps Kardar, Zhang and Takeuchi (B056) first, and argues that a prize for ever better accuracy would reward a technique, noting that comb and ion control were already honoured and Ye was part of the comb story.
responses.response: I have not moved on KPZ, but I take your reply about novelty to be the real question and I have tried to answer it. My answer is that what the lattice clock recognises is not better accuracy, it is a change of regime: many atoms with a cancelled light shift, which is why the statistical gain exists at all. For KPZ I still miss independence in the experimental evidence. As you say, the confirmation of the distributions rests largely on liquid-crystal turbulence work by Takeuchi and Sano, and the committee would be crediting an equation from 1986 and one realisation of it while leaving out the exact solutions that gave the theory its precision and Parisi, who is outside the trio. I respect the conceptual centrality of KPZ and I would want a sharper reproduction record across other physical systems before I could prefer it to a result confirmed by a dozen laboratories.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, asks whether a clock is a discovery about nature or a technology, notes that B043 is the more first-of-its-kind statement, and says he relies on Kroll and me for the atomic-physics priority questions.
responses.response: I accept the reliance and I have tried to be careful about what I can assert. On discovery versus technology, I would draw the line at whether the new instrument exposes new physics. Millimetre-scale gravitational redshift in a single atomic sample, limits on varying constants and dark-matter couplings, and many-body effects inside the clock all came from the lattice regime, so I put it on the discovery side of that line, though I grant that it is nearer the line than IceCube. On B043, I defer to you and Danielsson on the maturity of the diffuse flux, and I would be comfortable with it as a second part in a later year. For this vote, however, the clocks have a pair of names that the whole committee already agrees on, and B043 does not.

responses.point: Eriksson keeps topological insulators (B015) first, as a verified discovery of a new state of matter confirmed in several material systems, and calls the clocks the strongest challenger though 'a superb measurement' whose central discovery is harder to place.
responses.response: Your emphasis on a state of matter is fair, and in physics terms B015 is the stronger statement of a conceptual discovery. My difficulty is the one you concede yourself: the trio leaves out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, who proposed the HgTe route that made the observation possible, and the 3D contributors, and with Zhang deceased I do not see a fair three-person credit. I would not agree that the fairness question only affects which names we choose, because a statutory prize that gives the proposal for the experiment to people outside the trio misstates where the discovery came from. I weigh that more heavily than the lineage with the 2016 prize. If you can show a credit set that stays within three people and survives that objection, I would read it with interest, but at present it does not.

responses.point: Danielsson moved lattice clocks to the top because discoveries come first and attribution here is cleanest, while noting that his own earlier first choice was the Higgs experiments with Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee.
responses.response: I agree that the clocks pass both of your tests, and I appreciate that you moved after the exchange and did not defend the opening ranking. I do want to correct one point of emphasis. The redefinition of the second that you mention among the supports is not something I would let carry the citation, because it has not happened and it is a metrological decision. The redshift measurement, the 10^-18 agreement between laboratories and the fundamental-physics searches are what we can show today. On B053, I still hold that the experimental discovery is of the highest importance, but I have not heard an argument that these three names made the 2012 measurement, and I would not vote for a credit that I would have to defend as leadership recognition.

uncertainties: The priority chronology of the magic-wavelength proposal, including the Paris proposals around Lemonde and the early work in the Ye group, is from memory and not checked against the original 2001 to 2005 papers.
Whether the committee will accept that the lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, since Ye is a laureate of the first and the subject area is the same.

Whether the citation can credit Katori for the concept and first clock and Ye for the accuracy and redshift results in a single sentence without implying that the Sr and Yb community did not contribute.
Whether discovery is the correct reading of a clock result for those colleagues who weigh the statutory word strictly.
statement.conflict_note: No change since round 1. I am a long-time collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored with the Lund and Ursula Keller groups, but I have no collaboration with Katori, Ye or their groups, so I see no specific conflict for B002. I work in atomic, molecular and optical theory and ask colleagues to weigh my views on B002, B052, B060 and B063 with that field loyalty in mind. I am not recused from any shortlisted part.
